why_how.text: Pavement lines tell you where passing and lane changes are allowed, so reading them correctly keeps every pass legal.
Line color tells you which way the traffic beside you is moving, which matters before you cross any line.

scenario.text: Dev is behind a slow truck on a two-lane road with a solid yellow line on his side of the center.

reasoning.text: Yellow lines divide opposite directions, and a solid yellow line on your side of the center line means do not pass.

result.text: Dev stays behind the truck until the marking and enough clear road ahead allow a pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an empty road ahead makes it fine to cross a solid line to pass.

correction.text: A solid line should not be crossed to pass, and a solid yellow line on your side means do not pass, however clear the road looks.

memory_support.text: Broken may pass; solid says stay.

prompt.text: Dev is behind a slow truck on a two-lane road, with a solid yellow line on his side of the center line. May he pass?

answer.text: No. Do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line.

rationale.text: Yellow lines divide opposite directions, and the solid one on his side rules out passing even with an empty road ahead.

lines.text: Lines show where passing is allowed.
Color tells you traffic direction.
Some places rule out passing.

narration.text: This lesson is about the lines painted on the road. Pavement lines and symbols tell drivers where lanes split, where passing or changing lanes is allowed, which lanes are for turning, where walkers cross, and where to stop. We will begin with the difference between broken and solid lines, then sort out what yellow lines and white lines each divide, and how to read the line on your left. After that we will look at the center of a four-lane road, the no passing zone on a two-lane road, and the solid yellow line on your side of the center. We will finish with why you do not pass using the shoulder.

lines.text: A broken line may be crossed to pass.
A solid line should not be crossed to pass.
Check the pattern before you pull out.

narration.text: The first thing to read is the pattern of the line. A broken line may be crossed to pass, while a solid line should not be crossed to pass. That one rule settles many passing questions. Suppose you are behind a slow car on a two-lane road. If the line beside you is broken, passing is open to you, as long as you can see enough clear road ahead. If the line is solid, the marking is telling you not to cross it to pass. Pavement lines exist to show exactly this, where passing or changing lanes is allowed, so the pattern of the line is the first thing to check before you pull out.

lines.text: Yellow divides opposite directions.
White divides the same direction.
Yellow on your left means oncoming traffic beyond.
Solid white often marks the right edge.

narration.text: Color is the second clue. Yellow lines divide traffic going in opposite directions, and white lines divide traffic going the same direction. You can use this from the driver's seat. If the line on your left is yellow, the traffic beyond it is coming toward you. If the line on your left is white, the traffic beyond it is going your way. A solid white line often marks the right edge of the road. So on a road with several lanes, the white lines between lanes separate drivers heading the same way as you, while a yellow line marks where the oncoming traffic begins. Reading the color tells you which way the next lane flows.

lines.text: Four-lane center: two solid yellow lines.
No passing zones sit on hills or curves.
Solid yellow on your side: do not pass.

narration.text: Now the places where passing ends. On a four-lane road the center is marked with two solid yellow lines, and you must never cross them to pass. On a two-lane road, a no passing zone is marked by a solid yellow line. It is placed on hills or curves where you cannot see far enough ahead, so finish any pass before you reach it. Do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line. And on any two-lane road, never pass without seeing enough clear road, even if there is no marking at all. The paint tells you where passing is ruled out, and the clear road ahead decides the rest.

title.text: The shoulder is not for passing

lines.text: Do not pass using the shoulder.
Drivers do not expect a car there.
They may pull onto it without checking.

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches drivers stuck behind a slow car. The shoulder can look like open space, but do not pass using the shoulder. The reason lies with the other drivers. They do not expect a car to be there, and they may pull onto the shoulder without checking. A driver ahead of you could move onto it just as you come alongside. Keep the passing rules tied to the lane lines instead. A broken line may be crossed to pass, a solid line should not be, and on a two-lane road you never pass without enough clear road ahead. None of those rules ever turns the shoulder into a place to pass.

lines.text: Two-lane road behind a slow truck.
Solid yellow line on his side.
May he pass?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dev is on a two-lane road behind a slow truck. The center is marked with a broken yellow line on the far side and a solid yellow line on his side. The road ahead looks empty. May Dev pass the truck here? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line. Yellow lines divide traffic going in opposite directions, so this pair marks the center of the road, and the line on his side is solid. An empty road ahead does not change that, because a solid line should not be crossed to pass.

lines.text: Broken may pass, solid may not.
Yellow opposite, white same direction.
Finish passes before no passing zones.

narration.text: To close, put the pieces together. Pavement lines tell you where lanes split, where passing is allowed, which lanes are for turning, where walkers cross and where to stop. A broken line may be crossed to pass, while a solid line should not be. Yellow lines divide opposite directions and white lines divide traffic going your way, with a solid white line often marking the right edge. Two solid yellow lines at the center of a four-lane road are never crossed to pass. Finish any pass before a no passing zone on a hill or curve, and do not pass using the shoulder. Next we move to lanes, crosswalks and stop lines.

why_how.text: Knowing where to stop and when to yield at a crosswalk protects the people crossing in front of you.
Each lane has a job, and the guide rules out backing up or stopping in a travel lane.

scenario.text: Sam misses his exit on a busy highway and thinks about backing up to reach it.

reasoning.text: The guide says never back up in a travel lane, and never stop in one either; keep going instead.

result.text: Sam keeps going to a place where he can safely turn around.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a quick stop in a travel lane is fine if it is only to drop someone off.

correction.text: Never stop in a travel lane, whether you are lost, broken down or dropping someone off; keep going until you can safely pull off.

prompt.text: Nina's passenger asks to be let out right away, and Nina is in a travel lane on a busy road. What should she do?

answer.text: Keep going until she can safely pull off, then let the passenger out.

rationale.text: Never stop in a travel lane, whether you are lost, broken down or dropping someone off.

lines.text: Where to stop for a stop.
Who crosses at crosswalks.
Which lane to use.

narration.text: This lesson moves from lines to lanes. First we will settle where to stop when a sign or signal requires it, and what crosswalks mark. Then we will look at yielding to pedestrians, including at intersections where no crosswalk is painted. Next come lanes with special jobs: the dual-use lane with turn and straight arrows, the shared center lane used by both directions, and the marked left-turn lane. Then two firm rules about travel lanes, never back up in one and never stop in one. We finish with lane choice when three or more lanes go your way, and why passing on the right is risky.

lines.text: Stop before the stop line.
Or before a marked crosswalk.
Crosswalks are where pedestrians cross.

narration.text: When a sign or signal requires a stop, stop before the stop line, or before the crosswalk if one is marked. Crosswalks mark the area where pedestrians are meant to cross the road, so stopping before the crosswalk keeps that space open for them. Yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or about to step into one. Stay alert at intersections without marked crosswalks too, because not every crosswalk is painted. A walker waiting at a corner with no painted lines can still be about to cross, and you yield to them just the same. The stop point and the crosswalk work together to protect the people crossing.

lines.text: Turn and straight arrows share one lane.
Both arrows lit: turn or go straight.
Only straight lit: wait to turn.

narration.text: Some lanes do two jobs. In a dual-use lane with turn and straight arrows, you may turn or go straight when both arrows show on the signal. The catch comes when only the straight arrow is lit. Then you must wait for the turn arrow before turning, even though the lane itself allows turns. Think of it this way. The paint on the pavement says the lane can be used for turning or for going straight, but the signal decides which of those moves is open right now. A driver who wants to go straight can go on the straight arrow, while a driver who wants to turn waits for the turn arrow to appear.

lines.text: Shared center lane: both directions turn.
Solid and dashed yellow on each side.
Marked left-turn lane: solid yellow, thick stripes.

narration.text: Two kinds of center lane look alike. A shared center lane is bordered by a solid yellow and a dashed yellow line on each side. It is used by traffic from both directions for left turns, or U-turns where allowed, and you turn out of it as soon as your path is clear. Because drivers from both directions share it, you do not linger there. A marked left-turn lane is painted differently. Marked left-turn lanes use solid yellow lines together with thick yellow stripes on the pavement. So the solid and dashed yellow border tells you the lane is shared by both directions, while thick yellow stripes mark a left-turn lane.

lines.text: Never back up in a travel lane.
Never stop in a travel lane.
Keep going to a safe place.

narration.text: Here is a trap. A driver who misses a turn or an exit often wants to fix it right away, by backing up or by stopping to think. The guide rules out both. Never back up in a travel lane; if you miss a turn or exit, keep going to a place where you can safely turn around. Never stop in a travel lane either, whether you are lost, broken down or dropping someone off; keep going until you can safely pull off. The answer in each case is the same: keep moving with traffic until you reach a safe place, then turn around or pull off there. Lost, broken down, dropping off a passenger or past your exit, the travel lane is never the place to stop or reverse.

lines.text: Three or more lanes: keep right except to pass.
Center lane if many cars enter the right.
Left-most lane is for passing.

narration.text: On bigger roads, lane choice matters. With three or more lanes going your way, stay in the right lane except to pass, but use the center lane if a lot of traffic is entering the right lane. On multi-lane roads the left-most lane is meant for passing. Passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you and may move over. So the pattern is simple to follow: travel to the right, pass on the left, and shift to the center when the right lane is busy with entering traffic. If you find yourself about to pass on the right, remember the other driver may not know you are there.

lines.text: Busy road, travel lane.
Passenger wants out now.
What should Nina do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nina is driving in a travel lane on a busy road when her passenger asks to be let out right away. There is no place to pull off just yet. Should Nina stop in the lane for a moment so the passenger can get out? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Nina should keep going until she can safely pull off, and let the passenger out there. Never stop in a travel lane, whether you are lost, broken down or dropping someone off. The same thinking covers a missed turn: never back up in a travel lane, but keep going to a safe place to turn around.

lines.text: Stop before the line or crosswalk.
Yield to people crossing.
Keep moving; never back up.

narration.text: To close, here is what this lesson covered. Stop before the stop line, or before the crosswalk if one is marked, and yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk or about to step into one, even where none is painted. In a dual-use lane, wait for the turn arrow if only the straight arrow is lit. A shared center lane serves both directions for left turns and is bordered by solid and dashed yellow lines, while marked left-turn lanes have thick yellow stripes. Never back up or stop in a travel lane. Keep right except to pass, and use the left-most lane for passing. Next we turn to officers and traffic lights.

why_how.text: Traffic lights and officers decide who goes at most intersections, so their meanings must be instant.
Flashing and steady lights look alike but mean different things, and mixing them up leads to the wrong stop or go.

scenario.text: Eli reaches an intersection where the traffic signal is dark, and no officer is directing traffic.

reasoning.text: A traffic signal that is dark or not working is treated as a four-way stop.

result.text: Eli stops and treats the intersection as a four-way stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a flashing red light like a steady red and waiting for a green that never comes.

correction.text: A flashing red works like a stop sign, while a steady red means stop and wait for green except for a permitted right turn.

memory_support.text: Flash red is a stop sign.

prompt.text: Omar comes to a signal flashing red in his direction late at night. What should he do?

answer.text: Treat it like a stop sign: stop, then go when it is safe.

rationale.text: A flashing red light has the same meaning as a stop sign; waiting for green belongs to a steady red.

lines.text: Officers come first.
Steady lights: red, yellow, green.
Flashing and dark signals.

narration.text: This lesson is about who controls the intersection. Traffic control covers signals, signs and pavement markings, and it can also come from police, highway workers or school crossing guards, whose directions you must follow. We will start with the traffic officer, whose signal comes before any sign or signal. Then we will go through the steady lights: red, the right turn on red, yellow and green. After that we will untangle the flashing red and flashing yellow lights from their steady look-alikes, see when signals flash in all directions, and finish with a signal that is dark or not working.

lines.text: Police, highway workers and crossing guards direct traffic.
Obey the officer over any signal.
Officer says stop at green: stop.

narration.text: Start with people. Traffic control covers signals, signs and pavement markings, and it can also come from police, highway workers or school crossing guards, whose directions you must follow. When an officer is directing traffic, always obey the officer over any sign or signal. So if an officer signals you to stop at a green light, you stop. The green light does not override the officer; the officer overrides the green light. A crossing guard or a highway worker directing you is part of traffic control as well. Whenever a person is directing traffic, their directions are the ones you follow.

title.text: Steady red and right on red

lines.text: Steady red: stop and wait for green.
Stop line, crosswalk or before the intersection.
Right on red after a complete stop.

narration.text: At a steady red light, stop at the stop line, the crosswalk or before the intersection and wait for green unless you are turning right. The right turn has its own conditions. After a complete stop you may turn right on red if no pedestrians or traffic are in the way, unless a No Right Turn On Red sign is posted. Three things must line up. You come to a complete stop, not a slow roll. The way is clear of pedestrians and traffic. And there is no No Right Turn On Red sign. If any one of those is missing, you wait for green like every other driver at the steady red.

lines.text: Steady yellow: red is coming.
Stop unless in or too close.
Green: go, but yield first.

narration.text: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red, so stop unless you are already in the intersection or too close to stop safely. Steady yellow is not a signal to speed up. It is a warning that red is next. A green light lets you go through, but first yield to vehicles and pedestrians still in the intersection. If a car or a walker is still in the intersection when your light changes, you yield to them first. So yellow asks whether you can stop safely, and green asks whether the intersection has cleared. In both cases the light alone does not settle the question.

lines.text: Flashing red works like a stop sign.
Steady red means wait for green.
Right turn on red is the exception.

narration.text: Here is a trap built on two red lights. A flashing red light has the same meaning as a stop sign. A steady red means stop and wait for green, except for a permitted right turn. The difference is what happens after you stop. At a flashing red, you stop as you would at a stop sign and then go when it is safe; there is no green to wait for. At a steady red, you stop and wait for green, and the only move open to you is a right turn after a complete stop with the way clear and no sign forbidding it. Read whether the red is flashing or steady before you decide.

lines.text: Flashing yellow: slow, go with caution.
Steady yellow: stop if you safely can.
Signals may flash in all directions.

narration.text: Yellow has the same split. A flashing yellow light means slow down and go ahead with caution. A steady yellow means the light is about to turn red and you should stop if you safely can. So flashing yellow lets you keep going carefully, while steady yellow is asking you to stop. Signals may flash in all directions during emergencies, at night, in periods of light traffic and at special events. When you meet a flashing signal at those times, the color tells you what to do: flashing red works like a stop sign, and flashing yellow means slow down and proceed with caution.

lines.text: Late at night.
Signal flashing red his way.
What should Omar do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Omar is driving late at night, and the signal ahead is flashing red in his direction. Signals may flash in all directions at night and in light traffic. What should Omar do when he reaches it? Work it out before reading on. Omar should treat the flashing red like a stop sign. He stops, and then goes when it is safe. He does not wait for a green light, because waiting for green belongs to a steady red. A flashing red light has the same meaning as a stop sign. Had the signal been dark and not working, he would treat it as a four-way stop instead.

lines.text: Officer over every signal.
Red, yellow, green in order.
Dark signal: four-way stop.

narration.text: To close, here is the order of control. An officer's signal comes before any sign or signal, and police, highway workers and school crossing guards all give directions you must follow. At a steady red, stop and wait for green, or turn right after a complete stop when the way is clear and no sign forbids it. A steady yellow warns that red is coming, and a green lets you go after yielding to anyone still in the intersection. A flashing red works like a stop sign, and a flashing yellow means go ahead with caution. A traffic signal that is dark or not working is treated as a four-way stop. Next come turn arrows.

why_how.text: Left turns cross oncoming traffic, so knowing whether the signal protects you or leaves the gap to you is vital.
Each arrow color tells you whether to turn, find a gap, get ready or wait.

scenario.text: Theo is waiting to turn left and the signal shows a flashing yellow arrow, with oncoming cars still moving.

reasoning.text: A flashing yellow arrow lets him turn, but only after a safe gap in oncoming traffic opens and while yielding to pedestrians.

result.text: Theo waits for a safe gap, checks for pedestrians and then turns.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a flashing yellow arrow like a green arrow and turning straight into oncoming traffic.

correction.text: A green arrow gives a clear path, while a flashing yellow arrow allows the turn only after you find a gap and yield.

memory_support.text: Green arrow goes; flashing yellow waits.

prompt.text: The left-turn signal changes from a green arrow to a steady yellow arrow as Lina waits to turn. What does that tell her?

answer.text: The green arrow is ending, so she should get ready to yield or stop.

rationale.text: A steady yellow arrow follows a green arrow and warns it will change to a circular green, a flashing yellow arrow or red.

lines.text: Permissive, protected, or both.
Red, yellow and green arrows.
Gap or clear path.

narration.text: This lesson is about left turns at signals. We will start with the three kinds of left-turn phase: permissive, where you must find a gap yourself, protected, where oncoming traffic is held for you, and the protected and permissive phase that alternates between them. Then we will go through the arrows one at a time: the steady red arrow, the steady yellow arrow, the flashing yellow arrow and the green arrow. Along the way we will separate two pairs that are easy to confuse, the green arrow versus the flashing yellow arrow, and the steady red arrow versus the steady yellow arrow.

lines.text: Permissive: circular green or flashing yellow arrow.
Wait for a big enough gap.
Protected: green arrow, oncoming held by red.

narration.text: Left-turn phases come in two basic kinds. In a permissive left-turn phase you get a circular green or a flashing yellow arrow and must wait for a big enough gap in oncoming traffic. Oncoming cars are still moving, so the timing is your job. In a protected left-turn phase you turn only on a green arrow while oncoming traffic is held by a red light. Here the signal has stopped the traffic coming toward you, and the green arrow gives you the turn. So the question to ask at every left turn is simple: is oncoming traffic held by a red light, or is it still moving and leaving the gap to me?

lines.text: Alternates between both kinds.
Green arrow: protected turn.
Circular green or flashing yellow arrow: pick a gap.

narration.text: Many signals mix the two. A protected and permissive phase alternates between a green arrow and a circular green or flashing yellow arrow, when you must pick a gap yourself. During the green arrow part, you turn while oncoming traffic is held by a red light, just as in a protected phase. During the circular green or flashing yellow arrow part, the turn is permissive, so you wait for a big enough gap in oncoming traffic. The same lane can give you both kinds of turn at different moments. Watch which indication is lit at the moment you arrive, because that tells you whether the gap is your job.

lines.text: Steady red arrow: stop and wait.
May still need to yield to pedestrians.
Steady yellow arrow: green arrow is ending.

narration.text: Now the arrows that slow you down. A steady red arrow means stop and wait for green or a flashing yellow arrow, and you may still need to yield to pedestrians. A steady yellow arrow follows a green arrow and warns it will change to a circular green, a flashing yellow arrow or red, so be ready to yield or stop. Put simply, a steady red arrow means wait, but a steady yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending and you should get ready to yield or stop. The yellow arrow does not tell you which of those three indications is coming next, so you prepare for any of them.

lines.text: Green arrow: clear path, proper lane.
Flashing yellow arrow: find a gap first.
Yield to pedestrians either way.

narration.text: Here is the trap that matters most. A green arrow lets you go the way it points, provided you are in the proper lane and no traffic or pedestrians are in your path. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn in the arrow's direction, but only after a safe gap in oncoming traffic opens and while yielding to pedestrians. Both let you turn, so drivers mix them up. The difference is who is clearing the way. A green arrow gives a clear path in its direction, while a flashing yellow arrow allows the turn only after you find a gap and yield. Treating a flashing yellow arrow like a green arrow means turning into moving oncoming traffic.

lines.text: Green arrow becomes steady yellow arrow.
Lina is waiting to turn.
What does it tell her?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lina is in the left-turn lane. The signal has been showing a green arrow, and now it changes to a steady yellow arrow. What is the steady yellow arrow telling her, and what should she be ready to do? Work it out before reading on. The steady yellow arrow follows a green arrow and warns that it will change to a circular green, a flashing yellow arrow or red. So the green arrow is ending, and Lina should get ready to yield or stop. A steady yellow arrow is different from a steady red arrow, which means stop and wait for green or a flashing yellow arrow.

lines.text: Protected: green arrow, oncoming held.
Permissive: find your own gap.
Red waits, yellow warns.

narration.text: To close, here is the full set. In a permissive phase you get a circular green or a flashing yellow arrow and wait for a big enough gap. In a protected phase you turn only on a green arrow while oncoming traffic is held by red. A protected and permissive phase alternates between the two. A steady red arrow means stop and wait, and you may still need to yield to pedestrians. A steady yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after a safe gap opens, and a green arrow lets you go the way it points from the proper lane. Next we learn sign shapes and colors.

why_how.text: Shape and color let you know what kind of sign you face before you can read its words.
Several shapes and colors look alike, so learning the pairs keeps you from mixing up school, no passing and warning signs.

scenario.text: Gabe sees a pennant-shaped sign on the left side of a two-lane road.

reasoning.text: A pennant marks a no passing zone, while a pentagon marks a school sign.

result.text: Gabe knows a no passing zone is ahead and does not start a pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the pennant and the pentagon and expecting a school when the sign marks a no passing zone.

correction.text: A pennant shape marks a no passing zone, while a pentagon marks a school sign.

prompt.text: Rae sees a yellow green sign shaped like a pentagon. What kind of sign is it?

rationale.text: A pentagon marks a school sign, and yellow green is reserved for school signs.

lines.text: Shape tells the sign type.
Color backs it up.
Some pairs look alike.

narration.text: Signs carry meaning before you read a word, through their shape and their color. In this lesson we will learn the shape code first: the octagon, triangle, pentagon, pennant and diamond, then the vertical and horizontal rectangles and the round sign or crossbuck. Then we will learn the color code, from red, white and black, yellow and yellow green, to orange, green, blue and brown. We will separate two look-alike pairs, the pennant versus the pentagon and yellow versus yellow green. We will finish with what many regulatory signs look like and what a red circle with a red slash means.

lines.text: Octagon is stop; triangle is yield.
Pentagon is school; pennant is no passing.
Diamond is a warning.

narration.text: Sign shapes carry meaning. An octagon is stop, a triangle is yield, a pentagon is school, a pennant is a no passing zone and a diamond is a warning. Each shape belongs to one job, so you can tell the job from a distance, or from the back of a sign at a corner. A driver who sees an octagon knows a stop is required before reading the word on it. A triangle means yield. A pentagon tells you a school sign is ahead, and a pennant tells you a no passing zone is coming. A diamond warns of something ahead. Learn the five as a set, so that no two of them get swapped in your mind.

lines.text: Vertical rectangle: regulatory sign.
Horizontal rectangle: guide sign.
Round sign or crossbuck: railroad.

narration.text: Rectangles come in two directions, and the direction matters. A vertical rectangle is a regulatory sign, a horizontal rectangle is a guide sign, and a round sign or crossbuck means railroad. Many regulatory signs are white squares or rectangles with black or red letters or symbols covering direction, lane use, turns, speed and parking. So a tall white sign is usually telling you a rule, such as a lane use or a parking limit, while a wide sign is guiding you. When you see a round sign or a crossbuck, think railroad. These shapes add to the five from the last slide to complete the shape code.

lines.text: Red: stop, yield or prohibited.
White and black: regulatory.
Yellow: warning. Yellow green: school.

narration.text: Sign colors carry meaning too. Red is for stop, yield or prohibited, white and black are for regulatory signs, yellow is for warning and yellow green is for school. Notice how color and shape agree. The stop sign is an octagon and red, the yield sign is a triangle and red, and warning signs are usually yellow diamonds. Both white and black are listed as regulatory sign colors, so a white sign with black letters is telling you a rule. Yellow green is reserved for school signs, which sets them apart from the plain yellow used for general warnings. Color gives you a second clue when the shape alone is unclear.

lines.text: Orange: construction.
Green: direction and distance.
Blue: motorist services.
Brown: recreation and cultural interests.

narration.text: The second group of colors tells you about the trip rather than the rules. Orange signs are for construction, green signs are for direction and distance, blue signs are for motorist services, and brown signs are for public recreation and cultural interests. So an orange sign means a work zone or construction ahead. A green sign tells you where a road goes and how far away a place is. A blue sign points to services for motorists. A brown sign points to public recreation and cultural interests. These four colors, added to red, white and black, yellow and yellow green, complete the color code.

lines.text: Pennant: no passing. Pentagon: school.
Yellow green: school. Yellow: warnings.
White and black: regulatory.

narration.text: Here is a trap built on two pairs. A pennant shape marks a no passing zone, while a pentagon marks a school sign. Both have pointed ends, so they are easy to swap. Colors have a similar pair. Yellow green is reserved for school signs and yellow for general warnings. So if a question pairs a pentagon with yellow green, the answer is a school sign, and if it pairs a pennant with a no passing zone, it is about passing. Both white and black are listed as regulatory sign colors. Keep each pair apart by its job: school, passing, warning or rule.

lines.text: Yellow green sign.
Shaped like a pentagon.
What kind of sign?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Rae is driving through town and sees a yellow green sign shaped like a pentagon. Before she can read any words, what kind of sign does she know it is? Work it out before reading on. It is a school sign. A pentagon marks a school sign, and yellow green is reserved for school signs, so the shape and the color agree. If the sign had been shaped like a pennant, it would mark a no passing zone instead. And if it had been plain yellow, it would be a general warning. Shape and color together tell Rae to expect a school sign ahead.

lines.text: Red circle and slash: not allowed.
No Trucks, No Bicycles, No U-Turn.
Shape plus color equals meaning.

narration.text: To close, one more symbol. A red circle with a red slash over a symbol means that action is not allowed, such as no left turn or no U-turn. No Trucks and No Bicycles are examples of prohibition signs alongside No Left Turn, No Right Turn and No U-Turn. Now the whole code fits together. Octagon stop, triangle yield, pentagon school, pennant no passing, diamond warning, rectangles for rules and guides, round or crossbuck for railroad. Red for stop, yield or prohibited, white and black regulatory, yellow warning, yellow green school, orange construction, green direction, blue services, brown recreation. Next we study warning signs.

why_how.text: Warning signs give you time to slow down and get ready before a hazard or special situation arrives.
Signs about entering and ending lanes tell you who must merge and who must yield.

scenario.text: Kai is driving in the right lane when he passes a Lane Ends Merge Left sign.

reasoning.text: The sign means two lanes become one, and the right-lane driver must merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane.

result.text: Kai finds a space, merges left and yields to the cars already there.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an Added Lane sign means you must make room for merging cars.

correction.text: An Added Lane sign means entering traffic gets its own new lane, so no merge is needed; it is the Merge sign that means entering vehicles may move into your lane.

memory_support.text: Added lane: own lane. Merge: yours.

prompt.text: Ali sees an Added Lane sign as a ramp joins his road. Must the ramp traffic merge into his lane?

answer.text: No. Entering traffic gets its own new lane, so no merge is needed.

rationale.text: The difference between the Added Lane and Merge signs is whether entering traffic gets its own lane or moves into yours.

lines.text: Yellow diamonds warn you.
Stops, signals and crossings.
Merges and intersections.

narration.text: This lesson is about warning signs. Warning signs are usually yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols, and they tell you to slow down and be ready to stop for a hazard or special situation ahead. We will look at signs that warn of a stop sign or traffic light ahead, and signs for school and pedestrian crossings, including a color change coming to the School Crossing sign. Then we will sort out three lane signs: Added Lane, Merge and Lane Ends Merge Left. We finish with the intersection signs: T Intersection Ahead, Intersection, Side Road Ahead, Roundabout Ahead and Side Road Railroad Crossing.

lines.text: Stop Ahead: a stop sign is coming.
Signal Ahead: a traffic light is coming.
School and pedestrian crossings: slow down.

narration.text: Some warning signs announce a stop. A Stop Ahead sign means a stop sign is coming on your road, and a Signal Ahead sign means a traffic light is coming; be ready to stop for either. Other signs warn of people crossing. At a School Crossing sign, slow down and watch for children crossing, and at a Pedestrian Crossing sign, slow down and yield to people in the crosswalk. The School Crossing sign is being changed to a yellow green color over a transition the guide says will take effect within ten years. Yellow green is reserved for school signs, so the new color matches the school role of the sign.

lines.text: Added Lane: entering traffic gets its own lane.
Merge: entering vehicles may move into yours.
Both warn of traffic from another road.

narration.text: Two signs warn of traffic joining your road. An Added Lane sign means traffic from another road gets its own new lane, so no merge is needed, while a Merge sign means entering vehicles may move into your lane. The Added Lane and Merge signs both warn of traffic entering from another road; the difference is whether the entering traffic gets its own lane or moves into yours. So at an Added Lane sign, the joining cars have a lane of their own and nobody has to squeeze in. At a Merge sign, be ready for entering vehicles to move into your lane, because they are coming over into the space you are using.

lines.text: Lane Ends Merge Left: two lanes become one.
Right-lane driver merges left.
Yield to traffic already in the left.

narration.text: Here is a trap. The Lane Ends Merge Left sign is not about traffic from another road at all. A Lane Ends Merge Left sign means two lanes become one, and a driver in the right lane must merge left and yield to traffic already in the left lane. Compare that with the Merge sign, which means vehicles entering from another road may move into your lane, and the Added Lane sign, which gives them a lane of their own. With Lane Ends Merge Left, the lane ending is your own road's right lane. If you are in it, the job of merging and yielding is yours, not the job of the drivers already in the left lane.

lines.text: T Intersection Ahead: your road ends.
Intersection: another road crosses yours.
Side Road Ahead: a road joins from the side.

narration.text: Several signs describe the intersection ahead. A T Intersection Ahead sign means your road ends and you must turn right or left. An Intersection sign warns that another road crosses yours, and a Side Road Ahead sign warns that a road joins from the side the sign shows. A Roundabout Ahead sign tells you to slow to the posted speed restriction and use the roundabout rules. A Side Road Railroad Crossing sign warns that tracks cross just beside an intersection, so take care crossing them. Each sign tells you something different about the shape of the road, so read it in time to choose your lane and speed.

lines.text: A ramp joins Ali's road.
Added Lane sign posted.
Must ramp traffic merge?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ali is driving along a highway when he passes an Added Lane sign, just before a ramp joins his road. Does the traffic coming off the ramp have to merge into Ali's lane? Work it out before reading on. No. An Added Lane sign means traffic from another road gets its own new lane, so no merge is needed. If the sign had said Merge instead, Ali should expect entering vehicles to move into his lane. The Added Lane and Merge signs both warn of traffic entering from another road, and the difference is whether the entering traffic gets its own lane or moves into yours.

lines.text: Yellow diamonds: slow and be ready.
Know who merges and who yields.
Read the intersection shape early.

narration.text: To close, warning signs are usually yellow diamonds that tell you to slow down and be ready to stop for a hazard ahead. Stop Ahead and Signal Ahead mean a stop sign or a traffic light is coming. At a school crossing, watch for children, and at a pedestrian crossing, yield to people in the crosswalk. An Added Lane gives entering traffic its own lane, a Merge sign means it may move into yours, and Lane Ends Merge Left means the right lane merges and yields. A T intersection ends your road, an Intersection sign means a road crosses, and a Side Road Ahead sign means one joins. Next come curves, speeds and road conditions.

why_how.text: Turn and curve signs tell you how much to slow before the road bends, and weather can make even the advised speed too fast.
Slow vehicles, soft shoulders and objects at the road edge are hazards you must spot early.

scenario.text: Ivy approaches a curve sign with an advisory speed plate on a snowy evening.

reasoning.text: The plate gives the recommended speed, and you should never go faster than it in rain, snow or ice.

result.text: Ivy slows to no more than the plate's speed, even though the curve looks easy.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a curve sign carries the same recommended speed as a turn sign.

correction.text: Turn signs and reverse turn signs point to a top recommended speed of thirty miles per hour or less, while a curve sign only says the advised speed is below the posted limit.

memory_support.text: Turns thirty; curves below the limit.

prompt.text: Ray comes up behind a tractor with a reflective orange triangle on its back. What does the triangle tell him about the tractor?

answer.text: It travels under twenty-five miles per hour.

rationale.text: A reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle means it travels under twenty-five miles per hour, as farm vehicles often do.

lines.text: Turn, reverse turn and curve signs.
Advisory speeds in bad weather.
Slow vehicles and road hazards.

narration.text: This lesson covers signs about curves, speeds and the road surface. We will start with three signs that look alike, the turn sign, the reverse turn sign and the curve sign, and the speeds each one points to. Then we will look at the advisory speed plate and why weather changes how you use it, the Exit Speed Advisory sign for ramps, and the large arrows and chevrons placed at sharp bends. After that we turn to the reflective orange triangle on slow vehicles, Slippery When Wet and Soft Shoulder signs, divided roadways, object markers and the Bicycle Share the Road sign.

lines.text: Turn sign: sharp turn, thirty or less.
Reverse turn: two turns, opposite directions.
Curve sign: below the posted limit.

narration.text: Start with the turn signs. A turn sign marks a sharp turn with a recommended maximum of thirty miles per hour or less. A reverse turn sign warns of two turns in opposite directions, the second possibly sharper, with a recommended top speed of thirty miles per hour or less. A curve sign is different. It marks a curve whose recommended speed is below the posted highway limit. So turn signs and reverse turn signs both point to a top recommended speed of thirty miles per hour or less, while a curve sign only says the advised speed is below the highway's posted limit. Read which sign you have before you choose your speed.

title.text: Curve speed is not turn speed

lines.text: Turn and reverse turn: thirty or less.
Curve: only below the posted limit.
Watch for the second, sharper turn.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Because turn and curve signs both warn that the road bends, drivers often give them the same speed. They do not share one. Turn signs and reverse turn signs point to a top recommended speed of thirty miles per hour or less. A curve sign only says the advised speed is below the highway's posted limit, without naming thirty. On a reverse turn, remember there are two turns in opposite directions, and the second may be sharper than the first, so the speed that fits the first turn may not fit the second. If a question asks which signs share the thirty miles per hour figure, the answer is the turn and reverse turn signs.

lines.text: Advisory plate gives the recommended speed.
Never exceed it in rain, snow or ice.
Exit ramps have their own advisory sign.

narration.text: An advisory speed plate on a curve or turn sign gives the recommended speed, and you should never go faster than it in rain, snow or ice, even if it feels safe in good weather. An Exit Speed Advisory sign shows the recommended speed for a highway exit ramp, so ramps get their own advised speed. At the bend itself, you may see more signs. A large arrow placed on the outside of a turn and chevron signs at curves both stress the need to slow down for a sharp change of direction. So the plate sets the speed, the weather caps it, and the arrows and chevrons remind you to slow for the bend.

lines.text: Reflective orange triangle on the back.
Vehicle travels under twenty-five miles per hour.
Farm and construction equipment often do.

narration.text: Some warnings ride on vehicles. A reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle means it travels under twenty-five miles per hour, as farm vehicles and construction equipment often do. Do not confuse it with signs of a similar look. A triangle-shaped sign by the road means yield, and orange signs are for construction. The orange triangle on the back of a tractor or a piece of construction equipment is telling you about that vehicle's speed. When you see one ahead, expect to close the distance quickly, because the vehicle travels under twenty-five miles per hour.

lines.text: Slippery When Wet: slick in wet weather.
Soft Shoulder: stay on the pavement.
Object markers: something at the edge.

narration.text: Several signs warn about the road itself. A Slippery When Wet sign warns of a road that gets unusually slick in wet weather, and a Soft Shoulder sign means do not drive off the pavement. A Begin Divided Roadway sign warns that a median or barrier will soon split the two directions of traffic, and End Divided Roadway warns that the split is ending. Object markers warn of something in the road or right at its edge, a reminder not to drift out of your lane. A Bicycle Share the Road sign warns that cyclists may be riding in the same lane as motor traffic, so expect to meet them in your lane.

lines.text: Tractor ahead on a country road.
Reflective orange triangle on its back.
What does it tell Ray?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ray is driving on a country road when he comes up behind a tractor. On the back of the tractor is a reflective orange triangle. What does the triangle tell Ray about the tractor? Work it out before reading on. It tells him the tractor travels under twenty-five miles per hour. A reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle means it travels under twenty-five miles per hour, as farm vehicles and construction equipment often do. It is not a yield sign, even though a triangle-shaped sign by the road means yield. And it is not a construction sign, even though orange signs are for construction.

lines.text: Turns thirty or less; curves below the limit.
Advisory plate caps speed in bad weather.
Orange triangle: under twenty-five.

narration.text: To close, turn and reverse turn signs point to thirty miles per hour or less, while a curve sign says the advised speed is below the posted limit. Never go faster than an advisory plate in rain, snow or ice, and use the exit advisory speed on ramps. Large arrows and chevrons stress slowing for a sharp change of direction. A reflective orange triangle marks a vehicle that travels under twenty-five miles per hour. Slippery When Wet means the road gets unusually slick, Soft Shoulder means stay on the pavement, divided roadway signs mark where a median starts or ends, object markers flag hazards at the edge, and cyclists may share your lane.
